method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry, caption, image and note. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch18 p796-804: auto-generated source checklist from existing 181 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 2x-3x zoom; any printed unit errors, ambiguous glyphs, or nonstandard expansions are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan. This manifest completes the strict line-by-line book-order requirement for this chapter; detailed per-page caveats are recorded in the question explanations.

Oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction, as with NSAIDs, hypercalcemia or hepatorenal syndrome. [Oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction (NSAIDs/hypercalcemia/HRS); otherwise pre-renal failure is non-oliguric. (Book p797]

The two broad mechanisms of ATN are: [Renal AKI — ATN: ischemia and toxins (the toxins being endogenous and exogenous). (Book p797)]

A patient with ethylene glycol poisoning has oxalate crystals in the urine. In the drug chart, ethylene glycol is classified under: [Ethylene glycol is listed in the ATN column with the annotation 'oxalate urine crystals'. (Book p798)]

elements.source: Acute interstitial nephritis is: [AIN: hypersensitivity reaction (T₄ mediated), causing reversible AKI. (Book p799)]
Fill up: AIN is a ______ reaction, T₄ mediated, causing reversible AKI. [AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction that is T₄ mediated and produces reversible AKI. (Book p799)]

Match the AIN clinical features — 1) Rash, eosinophilia  2) Renal failure  3) Edema and hypertension  4) Flank pain, haematuria, pyuria … A) Asymptomatic  B) Rare  C) Absent  D) Present with eosinophilia [AIN clinical features: rash and eosinophilia; renal failure may be asymptomatic; no edema or HTN; flank pain, haematuria and pyuria are rare. (Book p7]
Edema and hypertension are characteristically absent in acute interstitial nephritis. [AIN clinical features: no edema, no HTN (in contrast with glomerular and volume-overload AKI). (Book p799)]

A patient started on an antibiotic 10 days ago now has a maculopapular rash, eosinophilia and a rising creatinine with no oedema or hypertension. Which diagnosis fits? [AIN: hypersensitivity reaction with rash and eosinophilia, asymptomatic renal failure without oedema/HTN (maculopapular rash figure). (Book p799)]

Match the AIN investigations — 1) RFT  2) Urinalysis  3) Renal biopsy … A) Mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts  B) Interstitial infiltrates with a normal glomerulus  C) Impaired [AIN investigations: impaired RFT; urinalysis — mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts; renal biopsy — interstitial infiltrates with a normal glome]
The renal biopsy finding in acute interstitial nephritis is: [Renal biopsy in AIN: interstitial infiltrates + normal glomerulus. (Book p799)]
Fill up: The urinalysis in AIN shows mild proteinuria and occasional ______ casts. [Urinalysis in AIN: mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts (not RBC or muddy brown casts). (Book p799)]
The treatment of acute interstitial nephritis consists of: [Treatment of AIN: stop the insult; after 1 week, steroids (mainstay). (Book p799)]

In the treatment of AIN, steroids are started after: [AIN treatment: stop the insult, and after 1 week steroids are the mainstay — the delay allows spontaneous recovery from the hypersensitivity. (Book p7]

All but one of the following are features of AIN. Which is the odd one out? [AIN is characterised by the absence of oedema and HTN; rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts and interstitial infiltrates with normal glomeruli all belong to ]

Complete the NSAID pathophysiology flowchart — 1) NSAIDs act on PGE₂/PGI₂  2) Effect on RAAS  3) Final step … A) Stimulation of RAAS  B) ↑K⁺ excretion via aldosterone  C) (–) inhibition [NSAID flowchart: NSAIDs (–) PGE₂/PGI₂ → stimulates RAAS → aldosterone → ↑K⁺ excretion. (Book p799)]

A 60-year-old on long-term NSAIDs develops AKI with a urine output of 400 mL/day, FeNa of 0.7% and a K⁺ of 6.4 mEq/L. Which statement matches the book's description? [NSAID nephropathy clinical features: oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion. (Book p799)]

All but one of the following are features of NSAID-induced nephropathy. Which is the odd one out? [NSAID nephropathy: oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion; FeNa >2% indicates established ATN. (Book p799)]

Complete the aminoglycoside pathophysiology flowchart — 1) Cationic amino groups on the drug  2) Target  3) Intracellular effect … A) Anionic megalin  B) Accumulates in lysosomes after endocytosis causing oxidative stress  C) Binds anionic megalin in the brush border of the PCT [Aminoglycoside flowchart: cationic amino groups on the drug bind anionic megalin in the brush border of the PCT; after endocytosis the drug accumulate]

Aminoglycosides are taken up into proximal tubular cells by binding to: [Cationic amino groups on aminoglycosides bind anionic megalin in the brush border of the PCT, are endocytosed, and accumulate in lysosomes causing oxi]

A patient given gentamicin develops non-oliguric AKI on day 7 of therapy. Which drug-related pattern is described? [Aminoglycoside clinical features: non-oliguric AKI 5–10 days after the drug — hence renal function must be monitored in this window. (Book p799)]

How is aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity prevented according to the page? [Prevention: administer the aminoglycoside as a single dose, following concentration-dependent killing, rather than by sustained divided dosing. (Book ]
Aminoglycoside-induced non-oliguric AKI typically appears how long after the drug? [Aminoglycoside clinical features: non-oliguric AKI 5–10 days after the drug. (Book p799)]

All but one of the following are correct about aminoglycoside nephropathy. Which is the odd one out? [Aminoglycosides cause non-oliguric AKI (5–10 days after the drug), with the megalin-lysosome-oxidative stress mechanism. (Book p799)]

Both NSAID and aminoglycoside nephropathy involve active reabsorption pathways in the proximal nephron. [Aminoglycosides are endocytosed after binding anionic megalin in the PCT brush border; NSAIDs act by inhibiting PGE₂/PGI₂, stimulating RAAS. (Book p79]

elements.source: Match the three phases of ATN described — 1) Phase 1 tubular injury  2) Phase 2 tubuloglomerular feedback  3) Phase 3 … A) ↓GFR from adenosine-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction  B) Recovery  C) Loss of solutes and water [ATN phases: 1 — tubular injury with loss of solutes and water; 2 — tubuloglomerular feedback → ↓GFR; 3 — recovery. (Book p800)]

In ATN, the fall in urine output is mediated by: [ATN phase 2: ↓urine output from adenosine-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, with ↑S. phosphorus, ↓S. Ca²⁺, ↑mg²⁺ and hyponatremia all red]

Match each ATN electrolyte acid-base change — 1) Serum phosphorus  2) Serum calcium  3) Serum magnesium  4) Serum sodium … A) ↓ (hyponatremia)  B) ↑  C) ↓  D) ↑ [ATN phase 2: ↑S. phosphorus, ↓S. Ca²⁺, ↑mg²⁺ and hyponatremia, all grouped with the fall in GFR. (Book p800)]

Match the complications of ATN — 1) Uremia  2) Volume overload  3) Acidosis  4) Potassium … A) ↑K⁺  B) Present  C) NAGMA  D) Present [ATN complications: uremia, volume overload, acidosis (NAGMA — normal anion gap metabolic acidosis) and ↑K⁺. (Book p800)]
Fill up: The acidosis of ATN is described as ______. [ATN complications include acidosis (NAGMA) and ↑K⁺ along with uremia and volume overload. (Book p800)]

Hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI. [Note: hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI (indeed calcium falls and hyponatremia occurs), whereas hyperkalaemia and acidosis are chara]
A patient with ATN is in the recovery phase. Which phase number and description apply? [ATN phases are 1 — tubular injury, 2 — tubuloglomerular feedback with ↓GFR, 3 — recovery. (Book p800)]
All but one of the following biochemical changes are seen in ATN. Which is the odd one out? [In ATN, S. Ca²⁺ falls (↓); phosphorus, magnesium and uric acid rise with hyponatremia. (Book p800)]

Complete the sepsis pathophysiology flowchart — 1) Pre-renal component  2) Macrovascular change  3) Microvascular change … A) Predominant over ATN  B) Microthrombi + endothelial leak  C) Widespread systemic vasodilation [Sepsis flowchart: pre-renal (predominant) >> ATN; widespread systemic vasodilation (macrovascular) + microthrombi + endothelial leak (microvascular) →]

In sepsis, the pre-renal component predominates over ATN, and microthrombi with endothelial leak cause ↓↓ kidney perfusion. [Sepsis flowchart: pre-renal (predominant) >> ATN, with vasodilation plus microthrombi and endothelial leak reducing kidney perfusion. (Book p800)]

Match the sepsis ATN pathway — 1) ↑PAMPs, DAMPs  2) Next step  3) Result … A) Inflammatory cascade  B) Released in ATN  C) Oxidative stress [ATN arm of the sepsis flowchart: ↑PAMPs, DAMPs → inflammatory cascade → oxidative stress. (Book p800)]

Match the causes of sepsis-associated AKI — 1) Urosepsis  2) CRBSI  3) Diabetic nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis) … A) Urosepsis  B) Catheter related bloodstream infection  C) Cellulitis [Causes of sepsis in this section: urosepsis; CRBSI (catheter related blood stream infection); DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis); ]

The sepsis causes listed besides urosepsis, CRBSI and cellulitis are: [Causes list: urosepsis, CRBSI, DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis), renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative. (Book p800)]

In early sepsis, why may the skin feel warm despite poor end-organ perfusion? [Signs of poor end-organ perfusion: HR >90/min, cool skin (redirection of blood flow) — warm in the early phase — with ↓urine output and restlessness. ]

Match each sign of poor end-organ perfusion in sepsis — 1) Heart rate  2) Skin  3) Urine output  4) Sensorium … A) ↓  B) Restlessness  C) >90/min  D) Cool skin (warm early) [Sepsis clinical features (signs of poor end-organ perfusion): HR >90/min; cool skin (redirection of blood flow), warm in the early phase; ↓urine outpu]
The heart-rate threshold given among the signs of poor end-organ perfusion in sepsis is: [Signs of poor end-organ perfusion: HR >90/min, plus cool skin, ↓urine output and restlessness. (Book p800)]

All but one of the following are listed as causes of sepsis-related AKI. Which is the odd one out? [Listed causes: urosepsis, CRBSI, DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis), renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative state. (Bo]
The normal IVC diameter used to determine the amount of fluid required is: [Investigations in sepsis-AKI: IVC diameter 2–2.5 cm is normal and determines the amount of fluid required. (Book p800)]

Match each sepsis-AKI parameter with its interpretation — 1) S. lactate >1 mmol/L  2) S. lactate >4 mmol/L  3) IVC diameter 2-2.5 cm … A) Normal value, determining the amount of fluid required  B) Organ hypoperfusion  C) Severe sepsis [Investigations in sepsis-AKI: an IVC diameter of 2-2.5 cm is normal and determines the fluid requirement; lactate >1 mmol/L indicates organ hypoperfus]
A serum lactate above which value indicates severe sepsis? [Serum lactate >4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis, while >1 mmol/L denotes organ hypoperfusion. (Book p800)]

The passive leg raising test (PLR) is described as: [Passive leg raising test (PLR): a test for fluid responsiveness, marked obsolete in the book, illustrated by the graph with the 30 mL/kg VE fluid chal]

Match each sepsis investigation with its purpose — 1) IVC diameter  2) S. Lactate  3) Passive leg raising test … A) Assesses organ hypoperfusion/severe sepsis  B) Determines amount of fluid required  C) Test for fluid responsiveness (obsolete) [Sepsis investigations: IVC diameter (normal 2–2.5 cm) determines the amount of fluid required; serum lactate >1 mmol/L = organ hypoperfusion and >4 mm]
A patient in the ICU has a lactate of 5 mmol/L. According to the book this indicates: [Serum lactate >4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis (levels >1 mmol/L indicate organ hypoperfusion). (Book p800)]

The passive leg raising test as a test of fluid responsiveness is described as obsolete. [PLR is a test for fluid responsiveness, described as obsolete, while IVC diameter and serum lactate remain the listed investigations. (Book p800)]

All but one of the following are listed among the investigations for sepsis-associated AKI. Which is the odd one out? [The listed investigations are IVC diameter (2–2.5 cm normal), serum lactate (>1 and >4 mmol/L thresholds) and the passive leg raising test. (Book p800]
